nodes.label: 5 cm snap-to-grid editing
nodes.rationale: Everything snaps to 5 cm while dragging rooms, lamps and furniture and while resizing a room from its corner. Snapping keeps walls and furniture aligned and prevents slow coordinate drift, at the cost of sub-5 cm precision that a home plan does not need.

nodes.label: Isometric 3D preview with Lights on toggle
nodes.norm_label: isometric 3d preview with lights on toggle
nodes.rationale: The lit isometric cutaway validates that the 2D plan reads as a believable home and previews the lighting result before applying, without leaving the editor.

nodes.label: Air conditioners section
nodes.rationale: Air conditioners get their own list below lights because they are placed as room-level units with their own device linking, not as lamps.

nodes.label: Building dimensions and outdoor temperature
nodes.rationale: Wall height 2.6 m, inner wall thickness 1.25 m and outdoor temperature 29 C drive the 3D geometry and the thermal context shown by the panel; they are metre/second-order physical facts, not per-object styling.

nodes.label: Default camera azimuth and elevation
nodes.rationale: Azimuth 34 deg and elevation 47 deg define the default view. Walls facing the camera are cut away, so azimuth decides which side of the home is left open; exposing both as numbers makes the cutaway predictable instead of accidental.

nodes.label: House Control Edit Home window
nodes.rationale: A single macOS window combines a spatial floor-plan canvas with list-based and numeric inspectors so one plan can be edited both by dragging and by typing exact values.

nodes.label: Light, strip and opening markers on the plan
nodes.norm_label: light, strip and opening markers on the plan
nodes.rationale: Round orange dots mark point lamps while short colored bars along walls mark strip lights and wall openings; color and shape encode fixture kind at a glance. Exact meaning of the blue versus orange bars is not stated in the screenshot.

nodes.label: Home global settings inspector
nodes.rationale: Plan-wide values are kept in a dedicated Home inspector rather than on individual objects, so a selected room or lamp edits only its own properties.

nodes.label: Import and Export plan controls
nodes.rationale: The plan is a portable JSON document, so import/export lets a home be backed up, shared, or edited elsewhere instead of being trapped in app storage.

nodes.label: Lights sidebar grouped by room and type
nodes.norm_label: lights sidebar grouped by room and type
nodes.rationale: Each light is named with its room and kind (Living - ceiling, Living - floor, Living - strip, Kitchen - spots, Bedroom - table, Bathroom - mirror) rather than by device id, keeping the plan human-readable and mapping fixtures to Smart Life device capabilities.

nodes.label: 2D floor-plan editing canvas
nodes.rationale: The top-down plan is the authoring surface: rooms, furniture, lamps and ACs are direct-manipulation objects on a dark grid, with room names and metre dimensions overlaid so geometry stays legible while dragging.

nodes.label: Rooms sidebar with dimensions
nodes.rationale: Rooms are listed with name and size (Living 6.4 x 4.6 m, Dining, Kitchen, Bedroom, Bathroom) so a room can be selected and edited without hunting for it on the plan; the add button supports drawing new rooms.

nodes.label: Save & apply action
nodes.rationale: Edits stay staged until Save & apply, which writes the plan to disk and reloads the menu bar panel, so the running panel can never disagree with what the editor shows. It is the primary blue action, separated from Undo/Redo and Import/Export.

nodes.label: Smart Life demo mode badge
nodes.rationale: Demo mode lets the owner design and preview a complete home before any Smart Life account is linked, so editing never blocks on OAuth or device discovery.

nodes.label: Editor status bar summary
nodes.rationale: The footer reports 5 rooms, 11 lights, 2 ACs and 0 linked to Smart Life, making integration coverage visible while editing instead of only after opening the panel.

nodes.label: Undo and Redo controls
nodes.rationale: Direct manipulation of a whole home is easy to get wrong, so edits are reversible in-session before the explicit Save & apply commit.

nodes.label: Light → room · mount binding notation
nodes.rationale: 'Living · ceiling' composes the physical location as a two-part key; the same key is legible on the plan and in the device list, so binding a real lamp never requires renaming the plan object.

nodes.label: Save & apply action
nodes.rationale: Editing is staged as a draft and committed explicitly; Import…/Export… sit beside it for file-based plan exchange, keeping destructive or device-affecting writes behind a single primary button.

nodes.label: 5 cm snap-to-grid editing
nodes.rationale: Plan geometry snaps to 5 cm and rooms resize from a corner, keeping dimensions plausible against real-world measurements without a numeric-entry form.

nodes.label: Undo / Redo history
nodes.rationale: Structural edits (drag, resize) are frequent and cheap to misfire, so reversible history is offered before Save & apply instead of confirmation dialogs.

nodes.label: Isometric 3D room preview with 'Lights on' toggle
nodes.norm_label: isometric 3d room preview with 'lights on' toggle
nodes.rationale: Live lit render of the same plan gives immediate feedback on lamp placement and light temperature, which a flat 2D plan cannot convey.

nodes.label: Connections panel — 'Where your real lamps and air conditioners live'
nodes.norm_label: connections panel — 'where your real lamps and air conditioners live'
nodes.rationale: One card per smart-home ecosystem, each showing a capability sentence, a status line (green check + hub name + device count, amber 'Not connected', or an action prompt) and a chevron for drill-down. Status is expressed in words, not only color, so the panel is readable and scannable.

nodes.label: 2D floor plan canvas (Bedroom, Bathroom, Kitchen, Living, Dining)
nodes.norm_label: 2d floor plan canvas (bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, living, dining)
nodes.rationale: Grid-backed plan with rooms as filled blocks, furniture as outlined shapes and lights as colored discs (blue = window/strip highlights, orange = warm lamps, green = connected lamp). Selection and connection state are signaled by color directly on the geometry rather than in a side list.

nodes.label: Home Settings sidebar (rooms, lights, air conditioners inventory)
nodes.norm_label: home settings sidebar (rooms, lights, air conditioners inventory)
nodes.rationale: Flat, grouped, count-badged list (Rooms 5, Lights 11, Air conditioners 2) with inline add buttons; each light row shows its room·mount binding plus a link glyph when the entity is bound to a real device. Chosen over a tree because the list doubles as the canvas' object palette.

nodes.norm_label: house control — edit home (desktop editor screen)

The screen answers 'where do my real devices live?' while the plan is being edited, so device binding is visible during layout work instead of in a separate settings flow.

nodes.label: Per-Device Command Queue and Store Coalescing
nodes.norm_label: per-device command queue and store coalescing
nodes.rationale: AppDelegate queues commands per device, polls state and reports results to the panel, while web/src/store.js coalesces changes into few commands and rolls back ones a device refuses, so dragging a slider does not flood the cloud.

nodes.label: Capability to Tuya Data Point Mapping
nodes.norm_label: capability to tuya data point mapping
nodes.rationale: Value ranges come from each device's own specification, so bulbs with a 0–255 scale and bulbs with a 10–1000 scale behave the same, and an AC shows only the controls its device has a function for.

nodes.label: Tuya Error Codes 2001 / 2008 / 1109
nodes.rationale: 2001 offline, 2008 command or value not supported, 1109 invalid parameter (usually several IR keys in one request); each maps to a specific user action.

nodes.label: Infrared AC as Tuya Virtual Remote
nodes.norm_label: infrared ac as tuya virtual remote
nodes.rationale: An IR-blaster AC has no state of its own: Tuya keeps a virtual remote in the cloud and each change is a key press, so mode and temperature changes are two transmissions a second apart, nothing is sent while off, and the panel shows only what was last sent.

nodes.label: 2008 Refusal Replay
nodes.rationale: If the cloud answers 2008 the state it remembers usually differs from the app's, so the app re-sends its whole state (power, mode, temperature, fan) and tries once more; a second refusal means that remote has no code for the setting and the panel says so and reverts.

nodes.label: Why No Google Home, Alexa or SmartThings Yet
nodes.norm_label: why no google home, alexa or smartthings yet
nodes.rationale: Alexa exposes no interface for another app to switch devices in the account; Google Home's APIs are mobile-only behind a Cloud project, Google sign-in and App Attest, and its Home MCP server is US-only; SmartThings needs a registered OAuth app and 24-hour personal tokens. Home Assistant is the practical route instead.

nodes.label: Build Provenance Attestation Step
nodes.rationale: Runs only on a public repository, because GitHub does not store attestations for private repositories on free accounts; that is why 0.1.0 has only a SHA-256.

nodes.label: Draft Release Creation
nodes.rationale: The release is created as a draft with the disk image and its SHA-256, so a human checks it before it becomes public.

nodes.label: SHA-Pinned GitHub Actions
nodes.rationale: Every action is pinned to a commit SHA with a version comment, and checkout uses persist-credentials: false, so a retagged action cannot silently change what the release build runs.

nodes.label: Tag Matches MARKETING_VERSION Check
nodes.rationale: The tag must equal v<MARKETING_VERSION> from ios/Config/Base.xcconfig, so a release can never ship a disk image whose version disagrees with its tag.

nodes.label: Release Workflow
nodes.rationale: Builds the Mac app on GitHub's machines, not a developer's Mac, so no personal certificate leaves a laptop and every image can be attested; a tag push makes a draft release, a manual run only an artifact.

nodes.label: Build Provenance Attestation
nodes.rationale: Every release image is built by GitHub Actions from the tagged commit and carries a SHA-256 plus a signed provenance attestation, so users can verify origin without a paid signing certificate.

nodes.label: Mac Release Process: Tag to Draft Release
nodes.norm_label: mac release process: tag to draft release

nodes.label: Ad-Hoc Signing Instead of Notarization
nodes.rationale: Notarizing needs an Apple Developer ID, and that certificate carries a person's legal name inside every copy of the app. House Control ships signed ad hoc instead and earns trust the open-source way: all code public, releases built in public, and users can build it themselves.

nodes.label: Sponsor Button to README Support Section
nodes.norm_label: sponsor button to readme support section
nodes.rationale: GitHub's Sponsor button points at the README's support section, where the crypto addresses and QR codes live, so there is one canonical place for donation details.

nodes.label: Crypto Tips as Project Support
nodes.rationale: The app is free with no ads; tips in crypto fund more devices, platforms and fixes, and a star, bug report or pull request is stated to help just as much.

nodes.label: Live Activity Feed
nodes.rationale: Everything an assistant reads or does shows up as it happens, with sparkles in the panel and island, so the user can watch the assistant work.

nodes.label: App Store Edition XcodeGen Spec
nodes.rationale: This spec is the App Store edition (Home Assistant, Philips Hue, Apple Home only); the Smart Life edition includes this file and adds the module on top, so one project definition serves both editions.

nodes.label: Declared Bonjour Service Types
nodes.rationale: iOS only browses the Bonjour types an app declares, so _housecontrol._tcp (Mac sync), _hue._tcp and _home-assistant._tcp are all listed in NSBonjourServices.

nodes.label: HouseSmartLife Module Linkage
nodes.rationale: Only this edition links HouseSmartLife, and build-ios.sh refuses an App Store archive that contains it, so the unsupported Tuya path cannot leak into the App Store build.

nodes.label: Separate Bundle ID and App Group
nodes.norm_label: separate bundle id and app group
nodes.rationale: The Smart Life edition is its own app with io.github.0xprobabillity.HouseControl and its own App Group, so both editions can sit on one iPhone without mixing their widgets.

nodes.label: Smart Life Edition Spec
nodes.rationale: for TestFlight and own use only, never the App Store, because Smart Life is reached through the sign-in Home Assistant's Tuya integration uses rather than a Tuya API offered to apps.

nodes.label: Bundled web/dist Resource Folder
nodes.rationale: The Vite build of ../web lands in the app as the folder 'dist', so the phone ships the same web UI as the Mac.

nodes.label: src/main.js ES Module Entry
nodes.rationale: Plain ES modules loaded by the browser, with no bundler runtime beyond Vite, so the same page runs in the app's web view and in a dev browser.

nodes.label: Locked Mobile Viewport and Dark Scheme
nodes.norm_label: locked mobile viewport and dark scheme
nodes.rationale: user-scalable=no, maximum-scale=1 and viewport-fit=cover stop the page zooming and let it draw under the notch; color-scheme dark matches the app's fixed dark look.

nodes.label: Bonjour Types Must Be Declared
nodes.rationale: iOS only browses the Bonjour types an app declares, so Hue Bridges and Home Assistant servers were never found until _hue._tcp and _home-assistant._tcp were added to NSBonjourServices.

nodes.label: Two iPhone Editions
nodes.rationale: Smart Life lives in its own module (HouseSmartLife) linked only by the Mac app and the Smart Life edition, so the App Store edition never contains the unsupported Tuya interface.

nodes.label: render_home Tool
nodes.rationale: Returns a picture of the 3D model, whole or one room, so the assistant can check its own work.

nodes.label: XcodeGen-Generated Xcode Project
nodes.rationale: The Xcode project is generated from YAML by xcodegen rather than checked in, so targets, entitlements and settings stay reviewable in small files.

nodes.label: iPhone App That Needs No Mac
nodes.norm_label: iphone app that needs no mac
nodes.rationale: The whole home can be set up on the phone, so pairing a Mac is optional; a paired Mac only adds two-way sync.

nodes.label: App Store and Smart Life iPhone Editions
nodes.norm_label: app store and smart life iphone editions
nodes.rationale: Smart Life is reached through the sign-in Home Assistant's Tuya integration uses, not an API Tuya offers to apps, so it stays out of the App Store edition entirely; the editions are separate apps (bundle id and App Group) and can sit on one phone.

nodes.label: Mac-to-iPhone Sync over Bonjour and TLS
nodes.norm_label: mac-to-iphone sync over bonjour and tls
nodes.rationale: The Mac advertises itself with Bonjour and the two talk over TLS with a pre-shared key that only the QR code carries, so nothing goes through a server and a device that never saw the code cannot connect.

nodes.label: dns-sd Bonjour Announcement
nodes.rationale: The lab Home Assistant's own Bonjour announcements do not reach the network, so homeassistant.sh announces it with dns-sd in the same format; enough for House Control but not for a HomeKit Bridge.

nodes.label: Single Three.js Web UI Shared by Both Apps
nodes.norm_label: single three.js web ui shared by both apps
nodes.rationale: Both apps are a small native Swift shell (AppKit on the Mac, SwiftUI on the iPhone) around one Three.js web UI, sharing device clients and sync as a Swift package, so the 3D scene, panel, island, editor and AI Access window are written once while each platform keeps native chrome.

nodes.label: HomeKit Entitlement
nodes.rationale: com.apple.developer.homekit is requested on the iPhone app because the Mac cannot switch Apple Home devices.

nodes.label: Photo-Library Usage Description for Sign-In Code
nodes.norm_label: photo-library usage description for sign-in code
nodes.rationale: The sign-in code must be scanned by the Smart Life app on the very phone in hand, so the code is saved to Photos and scanned from there; the usage description states exactly that.

nodes.label: One Home Mixing Four Platforms
nodes.rationale: Hue lamps, a Home Assistant air conditioner and a Smart Life plug can sit side by side, and everything not linked stays simulated, so a home need not be replaced wholesale to adopt the app.

nodes.label: Home Assistant Integration
nodes.rationale: One local server reaches thousands of brands (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter, Nest, Xiaomi, Aqara, IKEA, Sonoff, SmartThings, Daikin, Mitsubishi, Tuya), and its long-lived token is the only credential needed.

nodes.label: Hue Trust-on-First-Use Certificate Pinning
nodes.rationale: The bridge's certificate is self-signed; the app trusts it the first time and remembers its fingerprint, so a different device answering at that address later is refused.

nodes.label: Philips Hue Integration
nodes.rationale: Talks to the bridge's own local API after a button press, with no Hue account and no internet connection involved.

nodes.label: Tuya Devices in Apple Home via HomeKit Bridge
nodes.norm_label: tuya devices in apple home via homekit bridge
nodes.rationale: Smart Life devices are not HomeKit accessories, so the recommended free route is Home Assistant's Tuya integration plus its HomeKit Bridge; Homebridge and Matter multi-admin are alternatives.

nodes.label: AES-GCM + HMAC-SHA256 Request Envelope
nodes.rationale: Requests are AES-GCM encrypted and HMAC-SHA256 signed, matching what Tuya's own client does.

nodes.label: Smart Life QR Sign-In
nodes.rationale: A User Code plus a QR scan with the phone app, requiring no Tuya developer account; it is the same sign-in the Home Assistant Tuya integration uses.

nodes.label: Alternative Tuya Cloud Project Client
nodes.rationale: A cloud project with Access ID, Access Secret and data center can be used instead, but the QR sign-in takes precedence and TuyaService.swift has seen far less real-world use than the QR route.

nodes.label: Four Device Platforms Mixed in One Home
nodes.norm_label: four device platforms mixed in one home

nodes.label: HomeKit Limited to App Store Mac Apps
nodes.norm_label: homekit limited to app store mac apps
nodes.rationale: Apple offers HomeKit to iPhone and iPad apps and to Mac apps only through the Mac App Store; since House Control is a direct download, the Mac can list Apple Home devices and link them but only the iPhone switches them.

nodes.label: Smart Life Sessions Cannot Be Shared
nodes.norm_label: smart life sessions cannot be shared
nodes.rationale: Tuya renews the session as it is used, so it cannot be handed between devices; Smart Life signs in separately on the Mac and on each iPhone, while Home Assistant and Hue connections sync over the encrypted link.

nodes.label: Swift Port of tuya-device-sharing-sdk
nodes.rationale: SmartLifeService.swift ports Tuya's open-source tuya-device-sharing-sdk, the library behind Home Assistant's Tuya integration, and presents the same client identifier to Tuya, so the app speaks a protocol that already works with that account type.

nodes.label: App Group and Keychain Entitlements
nodes.rationale: App Group and Keychain access groups are shared between the app and its widgets: the group holds the home they draw and the connections they use, so a widget can act without launching the app.

nodes.label: HouseWidgets App Extension Target
nodes.rationale: The iPhone widget extension is a separate app-extension target built from the shared ../widgets/Sources and embedded into the app.

nodes.label: Widgets Depend on HouseCore
nodes.rationale: The extension links the same shared package as the apps, so snapshot and action rules are one implementation rather than a second copy in the widget.

nodes.label: Sandboxed Widget Extension
nodes.rationale: WidgetKit requires the extension to be sandboxed with hardened runtime; the host app is not, so the extension is the only sandboxed component.

nodes.label: Mac Widget Extension (HouseWidgetsMac)
nodes.rationale: A macOS 14 app extension named HouseWidgetsMac, embedded into HouseControl.app by scripts/build-app.sh because the Mac app itself is a Swift package.

nodes.label: Widget State Regression Fix
nodes.rationale: Widgets could jump back to an older state when the app started with widget taps still queued; the queue is now applied against the current snapshot.

nodes.label: Push Event Subscriptions
nodes.rationale: Home Assistant events and the Hue bridge's event stream make a lamp switched from a wall switch, an automation or the Hue app show up within a second, instead of waiting for a poll.

nodes.label: 12-Second State Polling
nodes.rationale: While the panel is open the app reads every linked device's state every 12 seconds, so changes made in the phone app or on a wall switch show up; Tuya's cloud offers no local event stream.

nodes.label: Queued Action Expires After Ten Minutes
nodes.norm_label: queued action expires after ten minutes
nodes.rationale: Nobody expects a lamp to switch an hour later, and an action is only ever run for the home it was made in, so a stale queue cannot act on a different home.

nodes.label: App Group home.json with flock
nodes.rationale: The snapshot and action queue live in the App Group container and are read and written under one flock, so the app and a widget never see half of each other's work.

nodes.label: App Intent Tap Handling
nodes.rationale: A tap applies the change to the snapshot with the same rules as the panel's store (scenes, clamping, 'a white temperature drops the colour'), so the widget redraws with the result at once while the real command is queued.

nodes.label: Controls and Quick Actions
nodes.rationale: iOS 18 / macOS 26 controls (All Lights, Light, Scene, Air Conditioner) and icon quick actions put the common switches on the Lock Screen, Action button and long-press menu.

nodes.label: Darwin Notification Wake-Up
nodes.rationale: A Darwin notification wakes the running Mac app so it takes the queue within milliseconds instead of polling.

nodes.label: HomeSnapshot
nodes.rationale: Rooms, lamps, ACs, furniture footprints and scenes with their state are posted after every change, so a widget can draw the home without the app or the network.

nodes.label: iPhone Widget Direct-to-Platform Path
nodes.rationale: The iPhone app is usually not running, so the extension sends the change itself to Home Assistant, Hue and Smart Life using Keychain-group connections; Apple Home actions wait in the queue for the app to open.

nodes.label: Live Widgets and Controls
nodes.rationale: Every widget is live: tapping a lamp, scene or AC switches it without opening the app, on the Home Screen, Lock Screen, StandBy, Control Center and the Mac desktop.

nodes.label: Mac Widget Action Path
nodes.rationale: The app runs in the menu bar and runs each queued action through the panel, the same path as a click, so it reaches Smart Life, Home Assistant, Hue and the island, and the widget redraws with the real outcome.

nodes.label: render-widgets Still Renderer
nodes.rationale: Renders PNGs of every widget without WidgetKit, so widget design can be reviewed and screenshotted outside Xcode.

nodes.label: Widget Signing and App Group Identifiers
nodes.norm_label: widget signing and app group identifiers
nodes.rationale: The Mac uses a team-prefixed group so no provisioning profile is needed, and an ad-hoc release has no team so the group is the bare identifier; whether a sandboxed ad-hoc widget can read it is untested, hence the advice to build with a free Apple Development certificate.

nodes.label: 128-Bit Key in Every Path
nodes.rationale: Every address carries a random 128-bit key; without it every path answers 404, so the public tunnel address alone is not enough to reach the home.

nodes.label: Action Links (/do/…)
nodes.rationale: Opening an action link performs the action and answers with the new state, so even an assistant that can only browse pages can run the home.

nodes.label: Auto-Stop Timer
nodes.rationale: The link can stop itself after 1 hour, 8 hours (the default) or never, limiting how long a leaked address stays a house key.

nodes.label: Cloudflare Quick Tunnel
nodes.rationale: A free random https://….trycloudflare.com address that exists while cloudflared runs, so the assistant's servers can reach a Mac behind NAT with no Cloudflare account and no inbound port.

nodes.label: cloudflared Developer ID Check
nodes.rationale: If cloudflared is missing the window offers to download it from Cloudflare's GitHub releases and keeps it only if it carries Cloudflare's Developer ID signature.

nodes.label: edit_floor_plan Tool
nodes.rationale: A list of operations applied together, including furnish_room which replaces everything in a room, so a photo of a living room can become the room in 3D.

nodes.label: Loopback-Only Listener on Port 7419
nodes.rationale: House Control listens on the loopback interface only, so nothing on the local network sees it and the tunnel is the sole route in.

nodes.label: MCP Server over Streamable HTTP
nodes.rationale: Model Context Protocol at /<key>/mcp with JSON responses and no server-sent events, so Claude, ChatGPT and Claude Code can change the home itself, not only open links.

nodes.label: OpenAPI 3.1 Description
nodes.rationale: Exposes the same tools as plain HTTP + JSON for Custom GPT actions and agent frameworks, so using an assistant does not require MCP support.

nodes.label: What It May Do Permission Switches
nodes.norm_label: what it may do permission switches
nodes.rationale: Device control and 3D-home editing are separate switches that take effect immediately even while the link is live; turning devices off makes the link read-only.

nodes.label: Plan Edit Validation
nodes.rationale: Edits are checked before saving: unknown furniture, overlapping ids and rooms that do not add up are refused with a reason the assistant can act on.

nodes.label: Rate Limit and 4 MB Body Cap
nodes.norm_label: rate limit and 4 mb body cap
nodes.rationale: Requests are limited to 240 a minute and bodies to 4 MB, bounding what a misbehaving or hostile client can do with a valid key.

nodes.label: This Mac Only Reach
nodes.rationale: Skips the tunnel and serves http://127.0.0.1:7419/<key>, for assistants running on the Mac such as Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, LM Studio and scripts.

nodes.label: undo_floor_plan_edit Tool
nodes.rationale: Puts the plan back as it was before the last change, so an aggressive assistant edit is always reversible from the window or by the assistant itself.

nodes.label: AI Access
nodes.rationale: Give ChatGPT, Claude or any assistant a private link or MCP address served by the Mac itself; Stop or the auto-stop timer makes the address disappear, and device IDs and sign-ins never leave the Mac.

nodes.label: AI Access Privacy Model
nodes.rationale: The assistant's provider sees room and device names, their state and the floor plan, but never the Smart Life sign-in or real device IDs. Cloudflare relays the connection like any HTTPS proxy; 'This Mac only' avoids the tunnel entirely. Nothing is stored except the three settings and the link lives only in memory.

nodes.label: No Backend and No Telemetry
nodes.rationale: The app talks only to the platforms the user connects, with no telemetry and no backend of its own; the single exception is AI Access's Cloudflare tunnel, which the user switches on and off.

nodes.label: Changelog Section as Release Notes
nodes.rationale: awk extracts this version's CHANGELOG section and perl joins wrapped list-item lines; if no section exists it falls back to GitHub's generated notes.

nodes.label: Capture What the Preview Shows
nodes.rationale: The editor's 3D preview is tappable and the whole look can be written into the scene being edited, so building a scene is done by lighting the home rather than filling in fields.

nodes.label: Light Groups
nodes.rationale: A control shortcut rather than a device: a lamp keeps its own state and may sit in any number of groups; a control reaches only the lamps that can do it, so a plain plug switches with the rest and keeps its brightness.

nodes.label: Full Scene Editing
nodes.rationale: A scene no longer only switches things on and off: each light takes brightness, colour temperature and colour and each AC a target, mode and fan, chosen in the scene's form.

nodes.label: linked:true Device ID Redaction
nodes.rationale: Real device IDs are replaced by "linked": true, a plan the assistant writes keeps them as they were, and devices linked to hardware cannot be removed through the link.

nodes.label: Air Conditioners Schema
nodes.rationale: An AC hangs on a named wall at a default height of 2.2 m, with a 16–30 °C default target range and an optional thermometer for the room.

nodes.label: Metre Coordinate System (x east, z south)
nodes.norm_label: metre coordinate system (x east, z south)
nodes.rationale: Everything is metres seen from above with x growing right (east) and z downwards (south), heights in metres above the floor and angles in degrees, so a plan reads like a drawing.

nodes.label: Device link / sensor / tuya Objects
nodes.rationale: A light or AC becomes real when linked to a platform device; Smart Life keeps its own tuya object (deviceId, sensorId, optional codes.switch for a second gang) because its identifiers and data points differ. Device IDs identify hardware, so the link, sensor and tuya objects must be removed before sharing a plan.

nodes.label: Furniture Catalogue
nodes.rationale: Furniture is decoration only, with a fixed type list (sofa, bed, kitchen, plant and so on) plus per-type options such as width, colour and stools.

nodes.label: Light Groups Schema
nodes.rationale: A named set of lamps switched as one, with ids in the same space as rooms, lights and ACs so a group of the living room's lamps wants living_dining rather than living.

nodes.label: A Home Is One JSON Document
nodes.norm_label: a home is one json document
nodes.rationale: The 3D scene, the panel and the editor are all built from the document, so swapping the file swaps the home; it stays plain, stable and easy to generate or version.

nodes.label: Lights Schema
nodes.rationale: Six light types (ceiling, pendant, spots, floor, table, strip) with optional y, rot and length overrides; capabilities brightness/temp/colour are omitted for a plain smart plug that only switches.

nodes.label: Openings (door, window, open)
nodes.rationale: A gap in a wall given by two end points that must be horizontal or vertical; sill and head place a window, and an 'open' opening is a doorway or missing piece of wall.

nodes.label: Rooms as Axis-Aligned Rectangles
nodes.rationale: Rectangles keep wall generation, snapping and opening placement tractable; an L-shaped room is made of two rooms, and where two touch an inner wall appears on its own.

nodes.label: Scenes with '*' Wildcard
nodes.rationale: In both the lights and acs maps the key '*' applies to every device and a device's own entry overrides it, which keeps whole-home scenes short; a device the scene says nothing about is left out, so capturing never makes a scene reach further.

nodes.label: Plan Validation Errors
nodes.rationale: A plan that does not add up is never rendered half-way: the panel says what is wrong and where, and the editor shows the same in its status bar.

nodes.label: Home Assistant demo Integration
nodes.rationale: The demo integration adds lights (dimmable, white, colour), thermostats / heat pumps and temperature sensors that answer like real ones, giving every capability the app maps.

nodes.label: HTTP Server Port 8123
nodes.rationale: 8123 is Home Assistant's default port, so the lab is found and addressed exactly like a real server.

nodes.label: Lab Home Assistant
nodes.rationale: A real Home Assistant installed into tools/lab/.ha on first run (about 1 GB) with demo devices covering every colour mode, three climate devices, fans and a thermometer; it prints its address and an access token.

nodes.label: Lab HomeKit Bridge
nodes.rationale: Built on HAP-NodeJS with lamps, a plug, two air conditioners and a thermometer, added to the Home app with setup code 031-45-154.

nodes.label: Lab Hue Bridge Emulator
nodes.rationale: Five lamps of different kinds in three rooms plus a motion sensor with a thermometer; Enter emulates the link button, or --auto pairs without interaction for tests.

nodes.label: The Lab: Pretend Smart Homes
nodes.rationale: Each harness runs on the Mac, is found by the app's real discovery, speaks the real protocol and prints every command, so the app can be built and tested without owning hardware.

nodes.label: ServiceTests Against the Lab
nodes.rationale: Unit tests cover translation to and from each platform and the hub's routing; ServiceTests additionally run against a live lab HA and Hue emulator via HOUSE_TEST_* variables.

nodes.label: Simulated Devices Until Sign-In
nodes.rationale: Until a platform is connected every device is simulated, so the app and its demo plans can be tried end to end before any hardware or account exists.

nodes.label: Bluetooth Integration Stub
nodes.rationale: Run as a plain process on macOS, Home Assistant cannot use Bluetooth because macOS would stop it, so the lab replaces that integration with a stub in homeassistant/custom_components/bluetooth.

nodes.label: Open at Login
nodes.rationale: Implemented as the app's entry under System Settings' Login Items, so the system owns the switch and the login item follows the app when it is moved.

nodes.label: Camera-Facing Walls Cut Away
nodes.rationale: Walls facing the camera are cut away and inner walls are drawn to interiorWallHeight, so the model stays readable from any azimuth; the azimuth therefore decides which side is open.

nodes.label: Floor Plan as One JSON File (plan.json)
nodes.norm_label: floor plan as one json file (plan.json)
nodes.rationale: Rooms, walls, doors, windows and furniture are built from a single JSON document, so swapping the file swaps the home, and it can be written by hand, versioned, exported or imported.

nodes.label: House Control
nodes.rationale: A home as a live 3D model in the Mac menu bar, around the notch and on the iPhone, controlling lights and air conditioners through Smart Life, Home Assistant, Philips Hue and Apple Home. A small native Swift shell around one Three.js web UI, with no frameworks, no Electron, no server and no account of its own.

nodes.label: The Island Around the Notch
nodes.rationale: A black tab grows out of the MacBook notch and springs open on hover with the 3D model, scenes and devices. It peeks out to report changes but never takes the keyboard from the app in use.

nodes.label: Menu Bar Panel
nodes.rationale: Click the house icon and a panel drops down; click anywhere else and it is gone. There is no Dock icon and no main window, so the app lives where a quick control belongs.
